author: Ryan Zentko
title: DGRO: Better Returns, Lower Volatility Than S&P 500 - iShares Core Dividend Growth ETF (NYSEARCA:DGRO) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Passive investing is still one of the best strategies for long term wealth accumulation, even with the return of volatility to the overall market. Active investing tends to underperform , and index funds and ETFs have their places in investor’s portfolios.
For 2019, I’m planning to quickly fund my Roth IRA, and iShares Core Dividend Growth ETF ( DGRO ) is one of the ETFs I already own, and plan to continue to contribute to. Dividend growth investing is an excellent investing approach, and DGRO is one of the best ETFs in this area. Unlike several dividend focused ETFs, DGRO offers capital appreciation that competes with, and often beats the S&P 500, while offering a higher dividend yield and lower volatility. For 2019, DGRO is positioned to continue their outperformance, and can serve as an excellent core holding for portfolios.
Asset Management Strategy As an index fund, DGRO’s management strategy doesn’t have many rules or guiding principles like active funds do. DGRO tracks the US Market Index, and sticks to a couple additional rules.
First, DGRO focuses on companies with 5 years of dividend growth history. This allows the index to not only include dividend aristocrats such as Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Proctor & Gamble ( PG ), but also growing companies that just started offering dividends, such as UnitedHealth Group ( UNH ), Home Depot ( HD ), Apple ( AAPL ) and Visa ( V ), which all have ten years or less of dividend growth history. This separates DGRO from the similar Vanguard Dividend Appreciation Index ( VIG ), which doesn’t have any of those four.
Although having a shorter history may provide higher dividend growth risk, it also offers greater capital gains potential, as well as companies that have been aggressive with their dividend growth rates, such as Starbucks ( SBUX ).
In addition, DGRO offers no exposure to REITs, and only companies that offer qualified dividends. DGRO also limits exposure to high dividend yield sectors such as consumer staples and utilities, by capping dividend payouts at 75%. This leaves both sectors to take up 11% and 5% of the ETF, respectively. All of these rules lead to higher beta and more volatility than high dividend ETFs, but DGRO makes up for it with higher capital gain potential.
Performance As a passive index, it is important to consider past performance. While past performance is only a factor, and past performance is not a guarantee of future results, for ETFs and passive funds, it remains an important factor to consider. As shown, DGRO does have slightly higher deviations than VIG since its inception. This can be explained by DGRO’s higher exposure to growth companies due to their guidelines above. So far, this has also translated to higher total returns. DGRO has also outperformed the SPY, while producing lower standard deviations. Overall, DGRO has a history of providing greater returns, while also providing less volatility than the S&P 500.

DGRO’s top five sectors by exposure are Financial Services, Healthcare, Industrials, Technology, and Consumer Defensive. Below, I will give a quick analysis of each of these, as well as where they are positioned to go for 2019.
Financial Services – DGRO is overweight financials compared to SPY and VIG. Almost half of DGRO’s sector exposure is made up of big U.S. banks. The financial sector ( XLF ) has had an abysmal quarter, and is down 14% YTD, while top holdings JP Morgan ( JPM ) and Wells Fargo ( WFC ) are down 8% and 23% YTD respectively. However, banks are now below their average valuations when compared to the SPY, as fears of a recession, rate hikes, and an inverting yield curve led to a sector wide sell-off. Stress tests reinforce bank’s abilities to survive a recession, and balance sheets and financial health are stronger than before the recession. This has lead famous investor Warren Buffett to increase his positions in large banks, likely viewing valuations attractive versus historical averages and economic outlooks. These factors combined show a strong potential upside for the financial sector, as valuations and sentiment are at lows.
Healthcare – Healthcare has been the strongest sector in 2018. The SPDR Healthcare ETF ( XLV ) is up over 4%, while the SPY is down 6%. This strength has largely been led by big pharma companies. In 2019, healthcare is positioned again to be one of the best sectors. Favorable tailwinds in demographics and spending represent strong secular growth, even if a recession is evident. This is coupled with likely continued gridlock in Congress, leading to major legislation risk remaining low. Their top healthcare holdings, Abbvie ( ABBV ), Johnson & Johnson, and Pfizer ( PFE ) were all on track for a strong year before a month ago. The combination of the market sell off and the Talc article caused JNJ to experience a sharp selloff, and Abbvie fell with the market, although their total return with dividends is still positive for the year. Strong healthcare exposure will likely contribute to DGRO’s performance in 2019, as investors will likely stick with these strong dividend stocks in a defensive sector. Top holding JNJ also has strong upside in terms of valuation, as the media exposure will likely fade as the year goes on.
Industrials – Many industrial stocks have been hit hard by the trade war, and this sector will likely lag if tariffs increase. Because of this, I prefer DGRO’s lower exposure to industrials than VIG’s overweight exposure. Political risks remain, although a trade truce could lead to major upside. DGRO is more diversified in this sector, as their top holdings in the sector, United Technologies ( UTX ) and Caterpillar ( CAT ), represent about 1.5% of the portfolio. Both of these stocks are down over 10% this year, as both have strong China exposure. Industrials can easily outperform with a trade negotiation and infrastructure bill, but this will remain a sector for investors to actively monitor. For DGRO, they hold an equal weighting in industrials, and with high short-term risk, I prefer their equal weight exposure to VIG’s overweight exposure.
Technology – Although technology is 13.5% of the portfolio, over half of their tech exposure is spread between Apple, Microsoft, and Cisco ( CSCO ). Apple’s short-term problems are well-known and well covered . However, valuation remains low, even when not accounting for their extremely large cash position. Although their short term future may be in doubt, innovations in wearables, services, and content present a bright future, and investors can expect apple to be aggressive in acquisitions if a bear market does come. Microsoft is another company with a healthy balance sheet and likely to be aggressive in a bear market. Satya Nadella has lead a complete turnaround of Microsoft, as this diversified company has exposure to social media (LinkedIn), gaming (Xbox), and cloud software (Azure). These segments will drive growth, and their multiple revenue sources should offer Microsoft strong recession protection. Lastly, Cisco is in the middle of a turnaround, as last quarter was their first time reporting upper single digit revenue growth in several quarters, with a strong 5% - 7% revenue growth guidance. Cisco’s infrastructure segment should remain recession resistant, although their ability to cross sell new products may be limited in a recessionary environment.
Overall, DGRO is invested in technology stocks with reasonable valuations, strong tailwinds, and healthy balance sheets. Despite having a 13.5% technology sector weighting, their holdings are top heavy, and represent established companies that will likely have lower volatility than the tech sector ( XLK ), as high valuations and legislative headwinds will affect other stocks in the sector.
Consumer Defensive – In a recessionary environment, the consumer defensive sector is a “flight to safety” move for some investors. Similar to technology, consumer defensive is another top-heavy sector for DGRO. Proctor & Gamble, Coke ( KO ), and PepsiCo ( PEP ) represent over half of the consumer defensive exposure. Coke and PG are dividend kings, and PepsiCo is a dividend aristocrat. Although the capital gain potential is limited, healthy cash flows, strong dividend growth records, and recession resistant businesses represent DGRO’s strong position in the consumer defensive sector. These blue chip investments are strong complimentary holdings to the fast growing, low yielding stocks such as Visa and Microsoft.
Investor Takeaway Since inception, DGRO has outperformed the SPY, while offering higher yields and lower volatility. Their distribution yield is currently at 2.44%, and their portfolio is positioned to offer exposure to companies with strong growth potential, companies with aggressive dividend growth policies, as well as several dividend aristocrats and dividend kings.
In the volatile tech sector, over half of their positions by weight are in established companies Apple, Microsoft and Cisco, which should help them avoid the extremely volatile short-term risk that accompanies tech. DGRO is overweight financials, which is a sector that has been hit hard and has low valuations, and is also a sector Warren Buffett is buying.
Overall, I prefer DGRO over their peers SPY and VIG. DGRO has a healthy balance of capital gain and dividend growth potential, and has more favorable sector distributions than VIG heading into 2019. Although a somewhat new fund, they also have a history of outperforming the S&P 500, and with a volatile market that is flirting with bear market territory, I believe DGRO is positioned to have a good chance of outperforming again.
